titleEn: When German workers sit on the board
facts: Under the 1976 Co-determination Act, employees of German companies with more than 2,000 staff elect half of the supervisory board seats; the chair, chosen by shareholders, holds a casting vote.

Works councils are elected separately from trade unions under the 1972 Works Constitution Act and must be consulted on dismissals, overtime, transfers and major workplace changes, but they cannot call strikes.
Coal, iron and steel firms operate under the stronger 1951 Montan rules, which give labour a director and near-parity on the board.

Supporters credit the system with Germany's relatively low strike rate and with negotiated restructuring; critics say works councils can slow decisions and sometimes cooperate too closely with management.
Board-level parity stops at 2,000 employees, so most family firms, start-ups and service workplaces have no parity board and many have no works council at all.
exampleEn: A machine-tool firm in Bochum wants to cut a night shift. Before any notices go out, managers must bring the plan to the elected works council, whose members include machine operators, and negotiate a social plan with severance and retraining.
qualificationEn: Boardroom parity only covers large corporations, and the real influence of a works council depends on how organised and confident its members are; plenty of small firms and service workplaces have neither body.

sources.title: Worker representation on corporate boards of directors

titleEn: The dual apprenticeship that trains Germany's trades
facts: In the dual system (duale Ausbildung), apprentices spend three or four days a week in a company and one or two days at a state vocational school (Berufsschule) for two to three and a half years.
Around 320 recognised training occupations exist, from industrial mechanic to bank clerk, and training contracts are regulated by the 1969 Vocational Training Act.
Chambers of commerce and crafts (IHK and Handwerkskammer) register the contracts, set examination standards and issue the final certificates.

Apprentices receive a training allowance that rises each year, and many stay on in the company afterwards; the Meister (master craftsperson) qualification is required to train apprentices in many trades.

Around half of school-leavers once entered the dual system, but the share has fallen as more young people choose university, and low-achieving pupils and migrants are over-represented among those who drop out.
exampleEn: A 16-year-old from a Realschule spends three days a week at a car-parts supplier and one day at vocational school, recording tasks in a training logbook that the chamber inspects before the final exam.
qualificationEn: The dual route is strong in industry and crafts but weaker in services, and regional training markets differ sharply; in big cities competition for the best places is fierce, while some rural firms cannot fill theirs.

titleEn: Ossi, Wessi and the identity that survived the Wall
facts: Ossi (easterner) and Wessi (westerner) became everyday labels after 1990, when the five new Länder joined the Federal Republic.
Ostalgie describes nostalgia for East German everyday life, from Vita Cola and Sandmännchen to Trabant cars, and it became a media genre with films such as Good Bye, Lenin! (2003).
Economic convergence stalled: eastern wages remain lower, large company headquarters are fewer, and the east lost population through out-migration, especially of young women.
The labels survive in jokes and insults such as Jammer-Ossi (whingeing easterner) and Besserwessi (know-it-all westerner), and they still surface in arguments about representation and money.
Regional identity in the east is not uniform: Saxony, Brandenburg, Thuringia and Berlin differ in economy, dialect and politics, and the old border runs through families as well as maps.
exampleEn: In a Leipzig office, a new colleague from Stuttgart is teased as a Besserwessi after rewriting a presentation, and she answers by asking whether everyone still meets at the Späti after work.
qualificationEn: The labels are a rough shorthand that hides big differences between eastern regions and generations; younger Germans often use them for jokes rather than to describe themselves, and many reject them entirely.

titleEn: Röstigraben: Switzerland's language border
facts: Röstigraben ("Rösti ditch") is the informal name for the cultural and political boundary between German- and French-speaking Switzerland, named after the potato dish associated with German-speaking households.
The term spread during the First World War, when German-speaking officers' sympathy for Germany clashed with French-speaking support for France and sharpened the language divide.
The divide shows up in referendums: French-speaking cantons have voted differently on issues such as joining the United Nations (accepted in 2002) and tightening asylum and immigration law.
Switzerland has four national languages — German, French, Italian and Romansh — and German-speaking Swiss use dialect (Schweizerdeutsch) in daily life, reserving standard German largely for writing.
The boundary runs through bilingual cantons such as Bern, Valais and Fribourg, where place names, school languages and local politics shift from village to village.
exampleEn: On the train from Zürich to Lausanne, colleagues switch from Swiss German to French at the language border, and with the language the greetings, small talk and meeting etiquette change too.
qualificationEn: The Röstigraben is a useful caricature rather than a hard line: language borders are gradual, city-versus-country differences cut across them, and younger bilingual professionals move between both sides daily.

expression.glossEn: the "Rösti ditch" — popular nickname for the political and cultural boundary between German- and French-speaking Switzerland

titleEn: Polderen: how the Dutch build consensus
facts: The polder model is the Dutch practice of consensus-based wage and labour negotiations between government, employers and unions, institutionalised in the tripartite Social and Economic Council (SER), founded in 1950.

The 1982 Wassenaar Agreement between unions and employers traded wage moderation and shorter hours for jobs and training, and is widely credited with the rapid fall in Dutch unemployment in the following decade.
The verb polderen now means to negotiate a compromise through long consultation, a habit linked to the centuries-old water boards (waterschappen) that managed shared flood risk.
Meetings often confirm deals prepared in advance: draft agreements circulate among members, and the formal gathering ratifies a compromise rather than debating it from scratch.
Critics say the model can delay decisions and leaves out migrants, gig workers and the self-employed, who are not represented at the consultation table.
exampleEn: A hospital's works council, management and union delegates spend weeks in polder talks over shift rosters and then present a compromise that none of the parties loves but all can defend to their members.
qualificationEn: Consensus takes time and does not cover everyone; in parts of health care, logistics and the platform economy, employers and unions bypass or replicate the model, and outsiders often experience it as a closed club.

titleEn: Belgium's pillars and the institutions people are born into
facts: Pillarisation (verzuiling) organised Belgian society into Catholic, socialist and liberal pillars, each with its own schools, newspapers, hospitals, unions, sports clubs and political party.
The system peaked in the first half of the 20th century; the 1950s school war over Catholic versus state education was settled by the 1958 School Pact.
The pillars thinned from the 1960s, but schools, universities, health funds and broadcasters remain segmented and party politics still follows the old lines.
Language legislation in the 1960s fixed the borders between the Dutch-, French- and German-speaking regions, and the federal reforms of 1970-1993 turned Belgium into a federal state.
For families, the result was — and partly still is — that school, doctor, bank and newspaper can all be chosen within one subculture.
exampleEn: A family in Leuven sends its children to a Catholic school, reads a Catholic daily and banks with a Catholic cooperative, while the socialist family across the street does the same through a different set of institutions.
qualificationEn: Pillarisation is mainly a historical frame now; most Belgians mix institutions and younger generations are less bound by it, while the separate and much more political language divide still structures the country.

titleEn: The 35-hour week and France's RTT days
facts: The two Aubry laws of 1998 and 2000, named after labour minister Martine Aubry, cut the statutory working week from 39 to 35 hours for companies above a size threshold.
The reform was presented as sharing work to create jobs and was phased in, with exemptions, negotiations and later adjustments by successive governments.

Employees whose hours fall below the legal maximum receive extra days off known as RTT (réduction du temps de travail), often attached to school holidays or used to make bridge days around public holidays.
Overtime is possible and has been expanded since 2002, so real hours differ widely; many managers are on annualised day counts rather than weekly hours.
Economists still debate the law's effect: some credit it with creating several hundred thousand jobs, while critics argue it added rigidity and that actual hours fell less than intended.
exampleEn: A Paris office worker counts her RTT days each January and spends them in May, adding a few days to a block of public holidays to make a week away without touching her annual leave.
qualificationEn: The 35-hour week mainly shapes salaried office jobs; many small firms, restaurants and self-employed people never applied it, and overtime rules have changed repeatedly, so the French working week is less uniform than the law suggests.

titleEn: Classes préparatoires and France's elite school pipeline
facts: Grandes écoles are selective higher-education institutions outside the main university system, training much of France's administrative, scientific and business elite, including École polytechnique, Sciences Po and the Écoles normales supérieures.
Entry usually runs through two years of intensive classes préparatoires (CPGE) after the baccalauréat, followed by competitive exams (concours) with very low admission rates.
The system has its own hierarchy and vocabulary: students are élèves, ranked by concours, and the top civil-service corps recruit directly from a handful of schools.

Critics describe it as a machine for reproducing elites, since admissions remain dominated by families in the upper professions, and reforms such as quotas and new preparatory classes for poorer areas have been contested.
In 2021 the École nationale d'administration (ENA) was replaced by the Institut national du service public as part of a modernisation effort.
exampleEn: A lycée student in Lyon spends two years in prépa with about 40 hours of classes and a written test every week, then sits the concours in spring hoping for one of a handful of places.
qualificationEn: Most French students never enter this system, and the grandes écoles sit alongside a mass university sector with different funding and prestige; the pipeline is influential but far from the whole of French higher education.

titleEn: Brick Lane and the making of Banglatown
facts: Brick Lane in east London became the heart of the British Bangladeshi community after migrants from Sylhet, then part of East Pakistan and later Bangladesh, settled there from the 1950s onwards.
The street's buildings record earlier migrations: Huguenot silk weavers in the 18th century, then Jewish immigrants, whose synagogue became the Brick Lane Jamme Masjid.
Bangladeshi curry houses and the Sunday market made the area famous, and from the 1990s local branding promoted it as "Banglatown".
Community life centres on the East London Mosque on Whitechapel Road, Bengali-language media and the Bengali New Year (Pohela Boishakh) street festival.
Gentrification, rising rents and Shoreditch nightlife have pushed many Bangladeshi families to Ilford and other parts of outer London.
exampleEn: On a Friday afternoon, market stalls sell sari fabric, vegetables and spices while office workers queue for bagels, the street's successive migrations sitting side by side.
qualificationEn: "Banglatown" compresses a complex community: Sylheti is the usual home language rather than standard Bengali, and most British Bangladeshis now live outside Tower Hamlets, so the street is a symbol as much as a neighbourhood.

titleEn: The pub and the working men's club
facts: The public house has been a licensed social institution since at least the 18th century; the 1830 Beerhouse Act deregulated beer sales and created a boom in small beerhouses, while later licensing acts and the 2003 Licensing Act shaped opening hours.
Pubs work as third places: they host darts and pool teams, quiz nights, union branch meetings, wakes and birthday parties, not only drinking.

Working men's clubs, founded in the 19th century, are members-only cooperatives run by a committee, with cheap beer and a concert room; they are especially common in northern England and the Midlands.
The trade has declined sharply, with thousands of pubs closing in the past two decades as younger people drink less and social life moves online and to cafés.
Food-led gastropubs and tiny micropubs have partly replaced the old drinking-only locals, changing who uses them and when.
exampleEn: In a South Yorkshire club, the committee noticeboard lists next week's bingo, a funeral buffet and the members' draw, and a pint costs less than in the town-centre bar.
qualificationEn: Drinking habits and pub survival differ enormously between cities, suburbs and countryside; the "local" is central to some neighbourhoods and irrelevant to others, and club membership is ageing.

titleEn: The Gaeltacht and the boundaries of Irish
facts: Gaeltacht (plural Gaeltachtaí) are the officially designated Irish-speaking districts, concentrated in counties Galway, Kerry, Donegal, Mayo, Cork, Waterford and Meath.
The Gaeltacht agency Údarás na Gaeltachta, established in 1980, supports employment, housing and language planning in these areas.
The Gaeltacht is small: roughly 2% of Ireland's population lives there, and even inside the districts Irish is the household language for only a minority.
Irish (Gaeilge) is an official language of Ireland and of the European Union, and Irish-medium schooling (Gaelscoileanna) has grown strongly outside the Gaeltacht.
The summer college (coláiste samhraidh) tradition sends teenagers to live with Gaeltacht families and speak Irish, a rite of passage for many Irish students.
exampleEn: In a Connemara shop, the shopkeeper counts out change in Irish and switches to English only when the customer answers in English, a small daily negotiation over language.
qualificationEn: Irish use in the Gaeltacht varies by generation and village, English dominates in many areas, and most Irish speakers today live in cities and towns outside the official districts.

titleEn: Siesta, sobremesa and Spain's working rhythm
facts: The siesta is a midday break historically linked to heat and to long agricultural working days, and it was once familiar across southern Europe, not only in Spain.
In contemporary Spain only a minority of workers take a real siesta; surveys show the practice is far more common among retired people than among full-time employees.

Many shops and hospitality businesses still split the day, closing around 13:30 or 14:00 and reopening around 16:30 or 17:00, with the main meal afterwards, while most offices have moved to a continuous day.
The sobremesa — lingering at the table after lunch to talk — is often the more important social ritual than sleep, especially at family meals.
Debate over ending the split day and aligning working hours with the rest of Europe continues, with periodic political proposals for a more European timetable.
exampleEn: A Madrid family's Sunday lunch runs from 14:00 to 17:00, with coffee and conversation filling the sobremesa long after the plates have been cleared.
qualificationEn: The siesta legend is overstated: in big cities and offices the working day is tight, regional habits differ, and calling Spain a nation of nappers is a caricature that Spaniards often find tedious.

titleEn: Euskara and the Basque language revival
facts: Basque (euskara) is a language isolate, unrelated to Spanish or any other living language, spoken by an estimated 700,000 to 800,000 people.

It is co-official with Spanish in the Basque Country and parts of Navarre, and education has driven its revival: many pupils now study through Basque in the model D stream, while community-founded ikastolas pioneered Basque-medium schooling.
The standardised written form, Batua, was developed in the late 1960s to unify dialects and is now the main form used in broadcasting and publishing.
Regional variation remains strong, with dialects such as Biscayan, Gipuzkoan and Souletin, and researchers still debate the language's origins.
Basque cultural life also runs through festivals, bertsolaritza improvised poetry and Basque-language media.
exampleEn: In a Bilbao school, children chat in Basque, switch to Spanish for a science explanation from a visiting teacher, and later join an after-school bertsolaritza club.
qualificationEn: Basque is strongest in Gipuzkoa and inland villages and weaker in metropolitan Bilbao and southern Navarre; bilingual Spanish-Basque life is the norm for most speakers, and revival has not reversed the long decline in some areas.

titleEn: Campanilismo and loyalty to the town bell tower
facts: Campanilismo means attachment to the local bell tower (campanile) and, by extension, fierce loyalty to one's own town or village rather than to a region or nation.
The sentiment is bound up with Italy's late unification in 1861 and the long history of independent city-states, which left strong civic pride and local rivalries.

Rivalries surface in sport, food and festivals: the Palio di Siena pits the city's contrade, or wards, against one another twice a year, and neighbouring Tuscan towns compete over wine, saints' days and football.
The comune, the basic municipality, is the everyday political unit and a focus of local identity, with its own mayor, council and patron saint.
Campanilismo is often used critically to mean parochialism, but it also sustains local volunteer associations, festivals and care for shared public spaces.
exampleEn: A young office worker in Arezzo can name the contrada symbols of Siena, mock Pisa's tower and explain the rules of a local wine cooperative, all in one conversation.
qualificationEn: Town loyalty is not the only Italian identity: regional movements such as Venetian or Sardinian nationalism and national media culture cut across it, and young people move between local, regional and national belonging with ease.

titleEn: Fika and the Swedish office coffee break
facts: Fika is the Swedish coffee break as a social institution, usually taken twice a day at fairly fixed times with coffee and something small to eat, often a cinnamon bun (kanelbulle).
The word is a reversed-syllable slang form of kaffe (coffee) and works as both noun and verb: att fika, vi fikar.
At many workplaces fika is scheduled in the morning and afternoon, managers are expected to attend, and skipping it can mark a colleague as unsociable.
The break is deliberately unhurried and is valued as a way to flatten hierarchy: conversation ranges over work and private life and crosses departmental boundaries.
Institutionalised fika is strongest in offices, schools and public bodies, and has been eroded by shift work, small businesses and remote work.
exampleEn: At 15:00 on a Stockholm office floor the kitchen goes quiet as the team gathers around a plate of cardamom buns, and the meeting about the new product waits until the coffee is finished.
qualificationEn: Not every Swede takes fika twice a day, and the ritual varies between workplaces; for newcomers it can feel compulsory, while remote and shift workers often miss it entirely.

titleEn: Silesian speech and the politics of regional identity
facts: Silesian (ślōnskŏ gōdka, also called gwara śląska) is a West Slavic speech variety used in Upper Silesia and recognised with its own ISO 639-3 code, szl, since 2007.
In the 2011 census about 500,000 people declared Silesian as the language spoken at home, and some 817,000 declared Silesian nationality, the largest minority identity in Poland.

Silesian identity mixes pride in coal and industry with a history of shifting borders under Prussian, German, Polish and Czechoslovak rule, and the Silesian Autonomy Movement campaigns for autonomy within Poland.
The language appears in local media, theatre and some schools as an extra subject, but it has no official status and its spelling varies between writers and organisations.
Silesian folk culture includes brass bands and dialect cabaret, and regional food and festivals are part of the identity.
exampleEn: A family in Katowice switches from standard Polish to Silesian at the kitchen table, and the grandmother's dialect words for tools and food are a source of both jokes and pride.
qualificationEn: Not everyone from Silesia identifies as Silesian, the language is stronger in old industrial towns than among newcomers, and census answers vary with how the question is worded and who is counting.

expression.glossEn: God bless — a traditional Silesian greeting used when meeting someone

titleEn: E-Estonia and the once-only digital state
facts: Estonia built a digital state on the X-Road data-exchange layer, launched in 2001, and an electronic ID card introduced in 2002 that carries digital signatures used in daily administration.
Public services follow a "once-only" principle: the state may not ask for data it already holds, and citizens can see which officials have accessed their records.
Estonia was the first country to hold national elections with online voting, in 2005, and today the great majority of tax returns are filed electronically.
E-Residency, launched in 2014, gives foreigners a digital identity and access to Estonian company registration and banking services without living in the country.
The system is not universal: older and rural residents use digital services less, and paper and in-person options remain available.
exampleEn: A freelancer in Tartu files an annual tax return in a few minutes, signs a contract with her electronic ID and checks the log to see which officials opened her file.
qualificationEn: Digital government works best for routine transactions; complex cases and elderly citizens still depend on offices and paper, and security concerns shape how the system is designed and debated.

titleEn: Blat and the Soviet economy of favours
facts: Blat is the Soviet-era practice of obtaining goods and services through informal personal networks and mutual favours (po blatu, "through connections") rather than through official queues or plans.
It thrived in the shortage economy: access to scarce goods, spare parts, housing, university places and medical care depended on who one knew.
Blat works through mutual obligation: a favour creates a debt to be returned later, often in a different currency of goods or services.
Scholars distinguish blat from bribery: money may be involved, but the core mechanism is reciprocal obligation, trust and ongoing relationships.
The practice persisted after 1991 and merged into post-Soviet business life, where personal connections still matter for contracts, permits and recruitment.
exampleEn: A factory manager in Nizhny Novgorod gets spare parts not from the official supplier but through a friend at another plant, and repays the favour months later by helping that friend obtain a holiday place.
qualificationEn: Blat is not uniquely Russian and has weakened as goods became abundant and markets formalised; it survives most in bureaucratic, medical and professional settings where access still depends on people rather than prices.

sources.title: Second economy of the Soviet Union

titleEn: Surzhyk and the mixed language of everyday Ukraine
facts: Surzhyk is mixed Ukrainian-Russian speech: village Ukrainian blended with Russian vocabulary and grammar, as well as Russian with Ukrainian elements.
It is named after a cheap bread made from mixed grain, and it emerged from centuries of bilingual contact and from Soviet-era urbanisation and Russification.
Surzhyk is widespread in central Ukraine, the east and the south; attitudes are mixed, often dismissed as spoiled language by purists but also a marker of local, unpretentious identity.

Since 2014 and especially after the 2022 full-scale invasion, many speakers have shifted toward Ukrainian, and surzhyk has become more visible in media and literature as a voice of everyday experience.
Linguists study it as an example of code-mixing without a stable standard, with patterns that differ by region, generation and education.
exampleEn: A shopkeeper outside Poltava switches between Ukrainian and Russian within one sentence, keeping Ukrainian grammar while dropping in Russian words for prices and goods.
qualificationEn: Not everyone speaks surzhyk, the mixing patterns differ sharply by region and generation, and the shift toward Ukrainian since 2022 has changed its social position without eliminating it.

expression.glossEn: a mixed Ukrainian-Russian speech variety, named after a mixed-grain bread

titleEn: Gecekondu and the making of Turkish city neighbourhoods
facts: Gecekondu (literally "put up overnight") are informal houses built on unused land at the edges of Turkish cities; the word also describes the settlements themselves.
They grew massively from the 1950s as rural migrants moved to Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir and Adana; by the 1980s a large share of city dwellers lived in gecekondu areas.
Repeated amnesty laws legalised the houses and gave residents title deeds, and municipal services were gradually extended, turning many settlements into built-up neighbourhoods.
Since the 2000s, urban transformation projects (kentsel dönüşüm) have demolished many gecekondu areas under earthquake-safety and redevelopment laws, replacing them with apartment blocks.
Gecekondu neighbourhoods have strong local networks, hemşehri (fellow-townsman) associations, mosques, coffeehouses and informal economies, and they are politically significant.
exampleEn: A family in an Istanbul neighbourhood remembers how the grandfather built their two-storey house in a single weekend in 1974, and how a later amnesty turned the squat into titled property.
qualificationEn: Gecekondu is not a uniform category: some settlements became legal and middle-class, others were demolished, and informal building and tenants' problems have not disappeared.

titleEn: Nemawashi: consulting before deciding in Japan
facts: Nemawashi (根回し), literally "going around the roots", is the informal groundwork of consulting stakeholders one by one before a formal decision is made.
It prepares a proposal so that the formal meeting confirms a consensus rather than opening a debate; a major change announced without nemawashi is considered rude and risky.
The term comes from gardening: transplanting a tree requires preparing its roots beforehand, the same metaphor as preparing people.
Nemawashi depends on hierarchy and on middle managers who shuttle between departments, so it is slow for big changes but can be quick for small ones.
Younger workers and foreign-managed companies often push back against the time it takes, especially in crises or when headquarters imposes a decision.
exampleEn: Before a Tokyo manufacturer announces a new supplier, an assistant manager spends two weeks visiting engineering, procurement and factory planning to listen and adjust the proposal, so the official meeting ends in five minutes.
qualificationEn: Nemawashi is an ideal as much as a rule: some managers skip it, foreign-owned firms use it selectively, and remote work has made quiet "walking around" harder.

expression.glossEn: preparing the ground by consulting each stakeholder before a formal decision

titleEn: Karoshi and Japan's limits on overwork
facts: Karoshi (過労死), "death from overwork", is a recognised social and legal problem in Japan, first publicised in the 1980s after the death of a 42-year-old employee in a shipping company.
Compensation decisions use working-hour thresholds: more than 100 hours of overtime in the month before death, or more than 80 hours a month over several months, is treated as work-related.
Karoshi now covers deaths from strokes and heart attacks triggered by long hours and suicides linked to work stress, known as karōjisatsu.
The salaryman — a male permanent employee of a large company, often commuting long hours and socialising with colleagues after work — became the emblem of the phenomenon.
Reforms since 2018 set overtime caps, generally 45 hours a month and 360 hours a year, and created a "work-style reform" agenda, but enforcement and small-firm compliance remain weak.
exampleEn: A mid-sized Osaka logistics firm now logs overtime monthly and sends the figures to the labour standards office, after a driver's stroke was ruled work-related.
qualificationEn: Karoshi statistics capture only the most extreme cases; many employees face chronic long hours without official recognition, while colleagues in the same companies may work ordinary weeks.

titleEn: Nunchi and the social art of reading the room
facts: Nunchi (눈치) is often translated as "eye-measure": the ability to read a room, sense others' moods and adjust one's behaviour without being told.
Nunchi is taught in childhood and valued in workplaces and family life; having good nunchi is praised, while being nunchi-eopda (without nunchi) means socially clumsy or inconsiderate.
The concept shapes Korean communication, which often depends on indirectness, shared context and status awareness rather than explicit requests.
In offices, nunchi affects when to speak in meetings, how to disagree with a senior and how much to socialise, and it can suppress open criticism.
The term now appears in self-help and career advice and is exported through Korean media as a cultural marker.
exampleEn: A junior employee notices the boss's frown and delays a question until after the meeting, while a colleague who misses the cue is gently teased for having "no nunchi".
qualificationEn: Nunchi is a skill that varies by person and situation, not a mystical Korean trait; younger Koreans sometimes push back against it, and international workplaces demand more explicit communication.

expression.glossEn: the ability to read a room's mood and adjust one's behaviour accordingly

titleEn: Hagwon and South Korea's private education economy
facts: Hagwon (학원) are private cram schools that supplement public education, operating after school and late into the night across South Korea.
They are central to the competition for university entrance, and parents spend a large share of household income on them; the private-education market is worth several trillion won a year.
Hagwon teach exam subjects but also English, maths, arts, coding and music, and some children attend several academies on the same evening.
The industry expanded rapidly from the 1980s and has been regulated repeatedly, including curfews on late-night study and caps on fees.
Successive governments have tried to reduce dependence on hagwon through after-school programmes and admissions reform, with limited success.
exampleEn: A Seoul middle-schooler leaves school at 16:00, eats dinner in a convenience store and attends two hagwon until 22:00, her mother tracking the schedule on a shared app.
qualificationEn: Hagwon culture is strongest in Seoul and metropolitan areas and among middle-class families; rural and low-income students have less access, which is at the centre of the policy debate.

titleEn: Hukou and the wall between city and countryside
facts: The hukou system is China's household registration system, formalised in 1958, which ties access to schooling, health care, housing and social insurance to a person's registered place.

Rural hukou holders who move to cities, often called migrant workers and numbering in the hundreds of millions, usually cannot use urban public schools or subsidised services in their destination city.

Reforms since the 2010s have eased restrictions in small and medium cities and introduced residence permits (juzhuzheng) with some rights, but mega-cities such as Beijing and Shanghai remain restrictive.
Changing hukou status depends on income, property ownership, qualifications and points systems, which means the poorest have the least chance of converting it.
The system is tied to urbanisation policy and social stability and remains one of the most debated institutions in Chinese society.
exampleEn: A construction worker from rural Henan leaves his children with grandparents because they cannot enrol in a Shenzhen state school; he sees them during the Spring Festival and by video.
qualificationEn: Hukou rules differ enormously by city and county, and families juggle documents and exceptions; the system has been loosened but not dismantled, and its impact varies with income and connections.

titleEn: Gaokao and the province-by-province exam race
facts: The gaokao (高考) is China's national college entrance examination, held once a year in June, and the main route into universities.
Scores are allocated by province, not nationally: quotas differ sharply, so a student in Beijing or Shanghai faces different competition from one in Henan or Shandong.
Since 2014 reforms have introduced subject combinations such as 3+3 and 3+1+2 in many provinces to reduce rote memorisation and broaden choice, though the core remains the exam.
Preparation dominates secondary school life through boarding schools, evening classes and private tutoring, and public slogans speak of "one exam determining a lifetime".
Exam week brings traffic controls, security and public attention, and top scorers are celebrated in local media.
exampleEn: A Henan high-school senior studies past midnight for two years, and the week before the exam her family books a hotel near the test centre so she can avoid the commute.
qualificationEn: The gaokao is not the only path, since vocational colleges, independent admissions and study abroad exist, but for most ordinary families it remains decisive, and provincial quotas make the stakes unequal.

titleEn: Guanxi and the work of personal connections
facts: Guanxi (关系) means personal connections and the network of relationships that carry social and economic obligations in Chinese society.
It works through reciprocity, trust and mutual obligation: a favour creates a relationship maintained over years through meals, gifts and exchange.
In business, guanxi can matter as much as formal contracts, as introductions, preferential treatment, access to officials and reliable suppliers often flow through relationships.
Guanxi overlaps with mianzi ("face"): face is the social standing that exchanges use and create, and causing someone to lose face damages the relationship.
Scholars distinguish guanxi from bribery, but anti-corruption campaigns since 2012 have changed how favours are conducted and made explicit corruption riskier.
exampleEn: A sales manager in Zhejiang asks an old university classmate to introduce him to a procurement director, then maintains the relationship for years with dinners and small, non-cash favours.
qualificationEn: Guanxi is not uniquely Chinese and varies by region and generation; urban professionals and foreign firms rely more on formal processes, and the line between a relationship and corruption is legally serious.

titleEn: Jugaad and the Indian art of the improvised fix
facts: Jugaad (जुगाड़) is a colloquial North Indian term for an improvised, low-cost workaround, a hack assembled from whatever is at hand.
The classic example is the jugaad vehicle: a makeshift motorised cart built from a water pump, tractor parts and a wooden frame, used to move goods and people in rural areas.
The word has spread into business writing and engineering culture, where "jugaad innovation" means frugal, fast and resourceful problem-solving for low-income markets.
Critics argue that jugaad can be a euphemism for low quality, unsafe or rule-bending solutions, and India's pre-1991 permit system, the Licence Raj, taught people to work around bureaucracy.
The term now appears in start-up jargon, design thinking and government rhetoric about self-reliance.
exampleEn: A village mechanic in Haryana straps a diesel water pump to a cart frame, welds a steering column and starts carrying passengers to the market, calling the result his jugaad.
qualificationEn: Jugaad is not a national trait: the term belongs to northern Indian speech, many businesses now value formal engineering over improvisation, and the line between clever and unsafe is blurry.

titleEn: Adda and the Bengali art of unhurried conversation
facts: Adda is a Bengali social institution: an informal, regular gathering for long conversation, usually in a café, tea shop, street corner or someone's home.
The word means both a place and an activity (adda kora, to hang out), and adda mixes gossip, politics, literature, humour and debate over tea.
Kolkata's coffee-house culture is famous for adda: the Indian Coffee House on College Street has hosted generations of students, writers and political activists.
Adda is associated with Bengali sociability; it can last hours and is often deliberately unrelated to any practical purpose.
Contemporary addas have moved to neighbourhood tea stalls, clubs and online chats, while rising rents have pushed out some traditional venues.
exampleEn: On a Sunday afternoon, a group of friends argues about the day's editorials over several rounds of tea at a neighbourhood shop, none of them in a hurry to leave.
qualificationEn: Adda is a Bengali urban phenomenon rather than an all-Indian one, and gender, class and age shape who takes part and where; many younger people now prefer cafés or group chats.

titleEn: Gotong royong and the kampung's mutual labour
facts: Gotong royong is the Indonesian ideal of mutual assistance: neighbours and kin working together on shared projects without payment.
It is celebrated in the national ideology of Pancasila and in the constitution's emphasis on social welfare, and it draws on village traditions in Java, Bali and elsewhere.
Households contribute labour to roads, bridges, mosques, funerals and weddings, often organised by the RT and RW neighbourhood administrative units.
Money and labour are pooled for independence-day celebrations and on kerja bakti cleanup days, and the practice continues in urban housing complexes.
Scholars note the tension between the ideal and reality: wage work, migration and elite capture of community projects have reduced voluntary participation in many places.
exampleEn: In a Jakarta kampung, men dig a drainage channel on a Sunday morning while women prepare snacks, and the neighbourhood head notes who came and who did not.
qualificationEn: Participation varies by neighbourhood, income and island; in crowded cities many residents contribute money instead of time, and the language of gotong royong is also used politically.

titleEn: Balikbayan boxes and the Philippine migration economy
facts: The balikbayan box is a large cardboard parcel that overseas Filipino workers send home, packed with groceries, clothes, toiletries and gifts for family.
Balikbayan also means a Filipino returning home; the box is central to the culture of migration and remittances and often arrives by sea after weeks of consolidation by freight forwarders.
Families track the boxes and open them together at Christmas or on a homecoming, distributing goods that may be cheaper or unavailable at home.
The practice reflects the scale of Philippine labour migration, with around ten million Filipinos living and working abroad, and it carries the emotional economy of absence.
Customs rules give returning residents some tax-free allowances, and critics note the consumerism and costs that box-sending imposes on poor households.
exampleEn: A Manila family opens four balikbayan boxes from Dubai in November, handing out chocolates, canned goods, shoes and a new towel set before the Christmas decorations go up.
qualificationEn: Not every migrant family sends or receives boxes, and remittance patterns differ by country and generation; the box is a symbol of migration more than a universal household routine.

titleEn: Kiasu and Singapore's fear of losing out
facts: Kiasu, from Hokkien kiaⁿ-su ("afraid to lose"), describes the anxious competitiveness of Singaporean society, from queueing for freebies to grabbing the best seats.
The word is a staple of Singapore English and popular culture; "kiasu parents" enrol children in multiple tuition classes, and "kiasu" behaviour appears at sales and school open houses.
Singapore's exam-driven education system, housing market and dense job competition are often cited as drivers of the anxiety.
Kiasu is marketed ironically: it has become a tourist and media trope, and campaigns and commentators periodically ask Singaporeans to be less kiasu.
Linguists treat kiasu as an example of how Hokkien, Malay, Tamil and English have shaped colloquial Singaporean speech.
exampleEn: On the morning of a school open house, parents arrive hours early, park along the road and queue for a place in the briefing room, joking that everyone is being kiasu.
qualificationEn: The label flatters and mocks at once: many Singaporeans dislike it, competition varies by class, and policy has tried to soften its most anxious educational forms.

titleEn: Taarof and the choreography of Persian politeness
facts: Taarof (تعارف) is an Iranian code of politeness and mutual obligation in which offers, invitations and compliments are made elaborately and initially refused.
The ritual follows predictable formulas: a shopkeeper refuses payment, the customer insists, and eventually a compromise is reached; refusing too quickly or accepting too readily can both be rude.
Taarof extends to greetings, seating, food, offers of help and paying for a taxi, and it signals respect and defines status between people.
The system can confuse foreigners and younger Iranians, especially when a taarof offer is sincere or when money is genuinely expected.
In business, taarof shapes meeting etiquette: complimenting a host's work and being offered tea more than once are normal.
exampleEn: A Tehran taxi driver refuses the fare and waves the passenger away, the passenger presses the notes into his hand, and the driver finally accepts after a short, smiling argument.
qualificationEn: Taarof is a stylised ideal rather than a script everyone follows; young urbanites and busy professionals often reduce it, and visitors should watch what locals do rather than rely on formulas.

expression.glossEn: an elaborate etiquette of offers, compliments and polite refusal

titleEn: Jirga and the authority of Pashtun elders
facts: Jirga is a council of elders that settles disputes and makes collective decisions in Pashtun society, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the former tribal areas, parts of Balochistan and Afghanistan.
Decisions rest on consensus among respected elders (masharan), with public proceedings guided by Pashtunwali, the customary code of honour and hospitality.
Jirgas handle land, blood feuds, marriage and family disputes, and their decisions are often enforced by social pressure rather than the state.
They run parallel to Pakistan's formal courts and have been criticised for excluding women and for sanctioning collective punishment, though women's jirgas exist in some areas.
Reforms after 2018 changed the legal status of the tribal districts, and formal courts increasingly compete with jirgas, especially in cities.
exampleEn: After a dispute over a boundary wall near Peshawar, both families bring elders together in a mosque courtyard, and the jirga announces a settlement before evening.
qualificationEn: Jirga is a Pashtun institution, not a national Pakistani one; its authority varies with local politics, and many disputes now go to formal courts instead.

titleEn: Grameen Bank and the village politics of microcredit
facts: Grameen Bank was founded by Muhammad Yunus in Bangladesh in 1983, building on a 1976 experiment lending small sums to poor women in Jobra village, Chattogram.
It pioneered group-based microcredit: borrowers form small groups, repay in weekly instalments, and social pressure substitutes for collateral.
The bank is owned overwhelmingly by its borrowers, with the government holding a minority share, and it reports millions of members, mostly rural women.
Microcredit has been credited with expanding women's economic activity and criticised for creating debt cycles and for not reaching the very poorest.
Yunus and Grameen shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize, and political conflict later led to his removal from the bank's leadership in 2011.
exampleEn: In a village in Tangail, a group of women meet under a tin roof to collect weekly instalments, and one uses a new sewing machine financed by a second loan to take on a school-uniform order.
qualificationEn: Grameen is not the whole microcredit story: repayment rates are debated, many households borrow from several sources, and the poorest often remain outside credit groups.

titleEn: Mahalla and the neighbourhood that registers your life
facts: Mahalla is a traditional neighbourhood institution in Uzbekistan and across Central Asia: a self-governing community of neighbours, often centred on a mosque, a tea house and shared courtyards.
In Uzbekistan the mahalla is formalised in law, with elected chairpersons and advisory councils that register residents and handle welfare, weddings and disputes.
The mahalla can mediate family disputes, organise charity and community work (hashar), and monitor young people, and it has been praised for social cohesion and criticised for surveillance.
State influence grew after a 2003 law and further decrees in 2005, when mahalla structures were expanded and given roles in cooperation with the police.
The mahalla survives as an everyday social unit even as apartment living and labour migration change its reach.
exampleEn: When a young couple in Tashkent plans a wedding, the mahalla chairperson helps set the guest list and enforces informal limits on spending and noise.
qualificationEn: Mahalla identity is strongest in old, low-rise neighbourhoods and smaller towns; in new apartment blocks the institution is weaker, and the state's role in it is contested.

titleEn: Mamak stalls and the late-night Malaysian table
facts: Mamak stalls are open-air food stalls run by Indian Muslim (Mamak) families, found on street corners and under trees across Malaysia and Singapore, especially in the evenings.
The stall is a multi-ethnic social institution: customers order roti flatbreads, teh tarik pulled tea and noodles, and sit at plastic tables until late.
Teh tarik is poured between two cups to make it frothy, and the drink is a symbol of the mamak.
Mamak stalls are sites of cross-ethnic contact, football-watching and late-night conversation, and they are licensed and regulated by local councils.
Kopitiam, the traditional coffee shop with Hainanese origins, is a parallel institution; together they reflect Malaysia's eating-out culture.
exampleEn: After a football match, Chinese, Malay and Indian friends share a table at a mamak in Kuala Lumpur, ordering roti canai and teh tarik and arguing about the game in their mixed everyday English and Malay.
qualificationEn: Mamak is an ethnic-religious category and some stalls are run by other groups; the social mix varies by neighbourhood, and licensing and halal questions shape who eats where.

titleEn: Harambee and Kenya's tradition of community fundraising
facts: Harambee ("all pull together" in Swahili) is Kenya's tradition of community self-help, in which people pool money and labour for schools, clinics, water tanks and church buildings.
It was promoted as a national motto by President Jomo Kenyatta after independence in 1963, and harambee fundraising events became a fixture of political and church life.
Citizens contribute at public harambees, politicians often compete to donate, and the practice finances a large share of local infrastructure and school fees.
Critics link harambee to corruption, patronage and pressure on poorer people to contribute beyond their means; it also reflects the retreat of the state from rural services.
The phrase appears on Kenya's coat of arms and is used by state institutions and political campaigns.
exampleEn: A village near Nyeri holds a harambee at the church to raise money for a new classroom, with a printed list of pledges read aloud and neighbours contributing cash, maize or labour.
qualificationEn: Harambee is strongest in rural areas and church networks; urban Kenyans often contribute through WhatsApp groups, and its ties to political patronage are widely debated.

titleEn: Ujamaa and the afterlives of Tanzanian socialism
facts: Ujamaa ("familyhood" in Swahili) was Julius Nyerere's socialist policy in Tanzania after independence, set out in the 1967 Arusha Declaration.
It emphasised collective village life in ujamaa villages, self-reliance, public ownership of the means of production, and equality in education and health.
Villagisation in the 1970s moved millions of people into planned villages and disrupted farming and food production; the policy is widely judged an economic failure.
Nyerere's legacy remains strong in the value placed on national unity, in the use of Swahili as a common language, and in a public-sector ethos.
The socialism was Africanised, drawing on extended-family solidarity rather than Marxist class theory, and Tanzania kept some room for private enterprise.
exampleEn: In a village school in Morogoro, teachers still invoke Nyerere's kujitegemea (self-reliance) when explaining why parents built the dormitory themselves.
qualificationEn: Ujamaa's ideals coexist with a market economy and deep inequality today; Nyerere is evaluated differently inside and outside Tanzania, and the word is often used rhetorically.

titleEn: Umuganda and Rwanda's monthly community work day
facts: Umuganda is Rwanda's monthly community work day: on the last Saturday of each month, from 8 to 11 in the morning, adults are expected to do communal work.
Projects range from cleaning streets and digging drainage channels to building houses for needy families and planting trees, with tasks assigned by local officials and workplaces.
The practice draws on a pre-colonial tradition of communal labour, but its current form was institutionalised after 1994 as part of reconstruction and "home-grown solutions".
After the work, communities hold a short meeting where leaders share information and citizens can raise issues.
Participation is strongly expected and absence can be noted; critics see both a genuine civic ritual and a tool of social control.
exampleEn: On the last Saturday of a Kigali month, neighbours clear a drainage channel behind the market, then sit in the shade for announcements about a new health-insurance scheme.
qualificationEn: Umuganda participation is higher in rural areas and among public-sector workers than among some urban residents; its compulsory edge is debated, and it is one of several state-promoted community policies.

titleEn: Equb and Ethiopian rotating savings groups
facts: Equb (also iqqub) is an Ethiopian rotating savings and credit association: members contribute a fixed sum regularly, and each member in turn receives the whole pot.
It is used for large expenses such as weddings, funerals, school fees, rent and medical costs, and it runs on trust rather than collateral.
Equbs exist in offices, churches, mosques and neighbourhoods, and among diaspora groups; larger ones often have written rules and a treasurer.
In Addis Ababa, equb participation is widespread among women traders and civil servants, supplementing formal banking that can be slow or inaccessible.
The equb is distinct from the iddir, a funeral association that collects regular dues for bereavement support.
exampleEn: Twelve market women in Merkato each contribute 500 birr a month, and each month one receives 6,000 birr to buy stock or pay school fees, with a list kept in a notebook.
qualificationEn: Equb depends on social trust and can fail if a member defaults; amounts and frequency vary widely, and iddirs or bank savings serve different needs.

titleEn: Almajiranci and Quranic schooling in northern Nigeria
facts: Almajiranci is a system of Quranic education in northern Nigeria in which young boys, the almajirai, are sent, often from poor rural families, to live with a Mallam and memorise the Quran.
Pupils typically survive by begging for food and alms, and the word derives from an Arabic term for a learner; they may receive little formal schooling.
The system dates from the spread of Islam in the region and was once a respected route to religious learning; poverty and population growth have strained it.

Estimates of the number of almajirai run into the millions, and northern state governments have debated reform, banning street begging in some states and trying to integrate the boys into formal schools.
Critics link the system to child neglect and to recruitment by radical groups, while defenders stress its religious and social role where state welfare is absent.
exampleEn: In Kano, a group of boys in patched kaftans moves between houses before dawn reciting verses and collecting leftover food, then returns to the Mallam's compound for lessons.
qualificationEn: Almajiranci is a northern Nigerian and Sahelian phenomenon, not a national one; its scale and abuses are documented, but many families see it as the only available religious education.

titleEn: Stokvel and South African savings clubs
facts: A stokvel is a South African savings club: members contribute a fixed amount monthly to a common pool, paid out in rotation or at year-end depending on the club's rules.
Stokvels are common among Black South Africans, especially in townships and rural areas, and are used for groceries, school fees, funerals, investments and family obligations.
Many stokvels have a constitution, a treasurer and a bank account, and burial societies are a related type focused on funeral costs.
The collective model provides discipline and companionship where formal banking can feel costly or distant, and the stokvel economy is estimated to handle billions of rand a year.
The institution grew under apartheid, when Black South Africans were excluded from many financial services.
exampleEn: A Soweto grocery stokvel of twelve women meets monthly in a member's living room, reads the minutes, collects 500 rand each and buys in bulk before Christmas.
qualificationEn: Stokvels range from informal neighbourhood pools to registered companies; not everyone participates, and the risks include mismanagement and fraud.

titleEn: Tro tro and the daily negotiation of Accra's traffic
facts: Tro tro are Ghana's shared minibuses and the main form of public transport in Accra and other cities; they run fixed routes but stop wherever passengers want.
The mate, or conductor, leans out of the door calling the destination, collects fares and signals stops by tapping the roof.
Trotro stations, known as lorry parks, are social and economic hubs with food sellers, mechanics and union offices.
Fares are negotiated with the unions and government, and rising fuel prices trigger fare increases and strikes.
Ride-hailing apps now compete with tro tro, and many minibuses carry slogans and religious messages painted on their bodies.
exampleEn: A young worker in Accra boards a tro tro from Circle to Madina, passes coins to the mate and knocks twice on the roof when she wants to get off at the junction.
qualificationEn: Transport varies by city: taxis dominate in some towns, and ride-hailing has changed Accra's market; not every Ghanaian uses tro tro daily.

titleEn: Boda boda and the Kampala motorcycle economy
facts: Boda bodas are motorcycle taxis found across Uganda and much of East Africa; the name refers to carrying passengers border to border between Uganda and Kenya.
In Kampala, riders organise into stages with chairmen, and they are the fastest way through traffic but also a major source of road accidents.
Riders are mostly young men, and the work is informal, with rented motorcycles, daily payments and fluctuating fuel costs.
Since the 2010s ride-hailing apps have formalised some boda boda service, and regulations require helmets, reflectors and licences, though enforcement is uneven.
The boda boda economy is politically important: riders are courted as a bloc at elections, and their associations negotiate with city authorities.
exampleEn: At a Kampala stage near the taxi park, a rider waits by his motorcycle, agrees a fare to Ntinda and weaves between cars while the passenger holds the spare helmet with both hands.
qualificationEn: Riding culture differs between Kampala, smaller towns and rural areas; some boda bodas are bicycles, and safety regulation is far from complete.

titleEn: La Sape and elegance as Congolese self-assertion
facts: La Sape (Société des Ambianceurs et des Personnes Élégantes) is a Congolese style movement whose followers, sapeurs, wear high-end designer clothes, often in vivid coordinated colours.
It began in the 1960s and 1970s in Brazzaville and Kinshasa, when returning migrant workers and musicians adopted the styles of European dandies, and it spread through both capitals and the diaspora.
Sape is a performance of elegance and self-respect in cities marked by poverty and political instability, and sapeurs compete at social events and parades.
Music carried sape abroad: Papa Wemba, a leading Congolese musician, was a famous sapeur and an icon of the movement.
Some sapeurs follow a sape rule of non-violence and cleanliness, styling themselves as gentlemen.
exampleEn: On a Sunday in Kinshasa's Matonge quarter, three sapeurs in tailored suits and polished shoes pose for photos outside a bar, joking about the price of their scarves.
qualificationEn: Sape is strongest in the two Congos and among diaspora communities; many young people cannot afford it and mix fast fashion, and the movement's ideals are not always lived.

titleEn: Fraternities, sororities and American campus life
facts: Greek-letter fraternities and sororities are social organisations mainly at US colleges, with recruitment (rushing), pledge classes and chapter houses linked to national bodies.

Membership is concentrated in the South and Midwest and at large public and private universities; historically many chapters excluded women, Jews and non-white students, and some remain criticised as exclusive.
Fraternities and sororities run social events, community service and alumni networks that can shape careers, and homecoming weekends bring alumni back for football, reunions and parades.
Hazing scandals, alcohol deaths and legal liability have led universities to suspend chapters and tighten rules.
Alternative social groups and a growing number of students who reject Greek life have changed the scene at some campuses.
exampleEn: A first-year student at a Big Ten university attends a series of rush events, accepts a bid from a sorority and moves into the chapter house in her second year, where homecoming week is the social high point.
qualificationEn: Greek life is a minority experience even at big universities, its character varies by campus and region, and not all fraternities are residential or party-centred.

titleEn: Koreatown Los Angeles and the business of belonging
facts: Koreatown in central Los Angeles is one of the largest Korean ethnic enclaves outside Korea, with Korean-language signs, restaurants, churches and 24-hour businesses.

It grew from the 1960s as Korean immigrants settled around Olympic Boulevard, and it became a symbol of Korean American life after the 1992 Los Angeles riots, when many Korean-owned shops were destroyed.
The area is densely mixed: Latino residents, especially Spanish speakers, make up a large share of the population, and Korean and Latino businesses and workers interact daily.
Koreatown's night-time economy, including restaurants, karaoke rooms and cafes, serves the wider city, and its image is used commercially far beyond the neighbourhood.
Rising rents and redevelopment have pushed some long-time residents out, and community organisations campaign for affordable housing and small-business protection.
exampleEn: At 11 p.m. in a Koreatown plaza, families, students and office workers eat at a 24-hour restaurant and then move to a karaoke room, with shop signs in Korean and Spanish along the same block.
qualificationEn: Koreatown is not only Korean and is not a self-contained community; its boundaries are fuzzy, its population is mixed, and the commercial brand hides housing and labour inequalities.

titleEn: Quebec French and the politics of fin de semaine
facts: Quebec French (français québécois) is the variety of French spoken in Quebec, with a distinct accent, vocabulary and idioms, and it is the mother tongue of roughly six and a half million people.
Language politics shaped it: the 1977 Charter of the French Language (Bill 101) made French the province's official language, restricted English-language schooling and changed the language of work.
Quebec French preserves archaic features and has its own standards; Joual is the name of the working-class Montreal variant that became a literary voice in the 1960s and 1970s.
English and French coexist in Montreal, but language remains politically charged, and Bill 96 in 2022 strengthened French requirements in public services and business.
French-Canadian communities in Acadia, Ontario and the diaspora share the language with their own accents and institutions.
exampleEn: A Montreal office worker says fin de semaine for weekend, while a colleague from Paris says week-end, and the difference becomes a running joke about who is more at home in the city.
qualificationEn: Quebec French is not one uniform accent, and Montreal, Quebec City and the regions differ; bilingualism is common but uneven, and language policy remains a live political conflict.

expression.glossEn: weekend — the everyday Quebec term where European French uses week-end

titleEn: Tianguis and the weekly rhythm of Mexican markets
facts: A tianguis is an open-air market in Mexico, held on fixed days in streets, plazas or fields; the word comes from Nahuatl tianquiztli, and markets are a pre-Hispanic institution.
Vendors set up stalls with plastic tarps and tables, usually specialising by product, and prices are negotiable.
Tianguis rotate on weekly schedules, so a neighbourhood may have a different market each day, and the día de plaza structures local shopping and social life.
In cities they provide affordable goods and employment and are regulated by municipal permits, while informal trade, sanitation and traffic create recurring conflicts.
Markets sustain regional food culture through quesadilla stands, herb sellers and seasonal produce.
exampleEn: In Oaxaca, the Thursday market takes over streets near the central plaza, and a family buys tomatoes, a clay pot and a bunch of herbs from the same vendor they have used for years.
qualificationEn: Tianguis differ hugely by region and city, some are elaborate market halls while others are improvised street markets, and supermarkets and gentrification have changed habits.

titleEn: Maquiladora work on Mexico's northern border
facts: Maquiladoras are export-processing factories, mostly along Mexico's northern border, that import components duty-free and assemble finished goods for export, especially to the United States.
The model expanded under the 1965 Border Industrialization Program and boomed after NAFTA in 1994, drawing millions of workers into electronics, auto parts, textiles and appliances.
Many workers are young women, and the factories shaped new urban settlements with dormitories, transport and canteens; work is fast-paced and turnover is high.
Plants juggle US customer demands, Mexican labour law and cross-border logistics, and production is often organised around just-in-time delivery.
Wages are low relative to US industry, and independent unions have faced obstacles, though labour reforms since 2019 have changed the legal framework.
exampleEn: In a plant in Tijuana, a line worker on the evening shift attaches wiring harnesses for a US carmaker while the shift leader posts the day's output target in Spanish and English.
qualificationEn: The maquiladora model is concentrated in the north, though some plants moved south; not all export factories are maquilas, and working conditions vary by sector and firm.

titleEn: Konbit and Haiti's tradition of shared farm labour
facts: Konbit (also written combite) is a Haitian tradition of collective agricultural work: neighbours gather to help one farmer clear, plant or harvest a field, working to drums and songs.
The host provides food and drink for the workers, and the favour is reciprocated when other members need help, making it a labour-exchange system rather than wage labour.
Similar traditions exist across the Caribbean and West Africa, and the roots are in African communal farming.
Konbit declined with rural migration, imported food and wage labour, but farmer groups and NGOs have revived it for soil conservation, tree planting and irrigation.
The word is also used by diaspora groups and organisations as a name for community mutual-aid networks.
exampleEn: In the Artibonite valley, a group of farmers clears a neighbour's plot before the rains, singing as they work in a line, then shares a midday meal of rice and beans.
qualificationEn: Konbit is remembered and revived more than it is universally practised; in many areas cash wages have replaced reciprocal labour, and the custom varies by region and crop.

titleEn: Lunfardo and the slang that made Buenos Aires sound
facts: Lunfardo is the slang of Buenos Aires, with roots in Italian, Spanish, French and African languages, developed in the late 19th century among immigrants and working-class porteños.
It appears in tango lyrics, literature and everyday speech: words such as che (hey), laburo (work), mina (woman), pibe (kid) and guita (money) are widely used in Argentina.
The name may come from lombardo (Lombard), and the slang was initially associated with criminals and the poor before intellectuals collected and celebrated it.
Lunfardo is not a separate language but a vocabulary and register that varies by age, class and neighbourhood, and modern Argentine slang adds layers from football, music and the internet.
Tango, declared intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO in 2009, helped carry lunfardo worldwide.
exampleEn: A building porter in Buenos Aires asks a teenager "¿Che, tenés laburo?" ("Hey, do you have work?"), and the teenager answers with newer slang that mixes lunfardo with internet terms.
qualificationEn: Lunfardo is porteño and Argentine rather than universal Spanish; some words fade while others spread, and the line between slang and standard speech is fuzzy.

expression.glossEn: hey — a vocative used to get attention, the most famous Argentine slang word

titleEn: Jeitinho and the Brazilian workaround
facts: Jeitinho brasileiro ("the Brazilian way") is the practice of finding an improvisational workaround to rules, bureaucracy or scarcity, often through personal relationships and charm.
Everyday talk distinguishes jeitinho from corruption: it can be a clever shortcut, a favour from a friend or a small rule-bending, and the boundary is debated.
The custo Brasil, the high cost of doing business and daily life from taxes, bureaucracy and logistics, is often cited as the reason jeitinho develops.
Anthropologists describe jeitinho as a social skill that depends on creating familiarity and navigating hierarchy, and it has been studied since the 1980s as a cultural pattern.
In offices, jeitinho can mean bypassing procurement rules, borrowing a colleague's credentials or negotiating a deadline informally.
exampleEn: A small-business owner in São Paulo needs a licence before a holiday; a friend at the town hall explains which form to bring and which queue to avoid, and the document is processed in one morning.
qualificationEn: Jeitinho is a stereotype with real content: many Brazilians dislike the label and insist rules should be followed, and using it to excuse corruption is contested.

expression.glossEn: a little way — an improvised, often relationship-based solution

titleEn: Vestibular, ENEM and Brazil's university entrance race
facts: The vestibular is the traditional Brazilian university entrance exam, used by universities to select students; its name refers to the entrance hall, and it combines multiple-choice questions with essays.
It was historically taken after high school, and private cram courses (cursinhos) became a national institution.
The ENEM national exam, created in 1998, has increasingly replaced or complemented vestibulars, and since 2010 it has fed the SISU system that allocates places at federal universities.
State universities such as USP and Unicamp keep their own vestibulars, while quotas for public-school and low-income students have changed the mix of admitted students.
Elite courses such as medicine, engineering and law remain highly competitive, and cursinho culture reflects the pressure.
exampleEn: A student in São Paulo attends a cursinho in the evenings while finishing high school, takes the ENEM and a university vestibular, then waits for the SISU placement list in January.
qualificationEn: The vestibular is being replaced piecemeal and rules differ state by state; the national ENEM route has broadened access but not eliminated the advantage of good schools and coaching.

titleEn: Minka and ayni: Andean reciprocal labour
facts: Minka (also minga) is an Andean tradition of communal work: a community turns out to build a road, clean a canal, repair a school or harvest crops, and the host provides food and drink.
It is rooted in Quechua and Aymara ideas of reciprocity and is found in Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador; in pre-Columbian times minka was used for public works such as terraces and canals.
A related concept is ayni, the reciprocal exchange of labour between households, especially in farming.
In modern Peru, minka is often organised for rural infrastructure and disaster response, and it is also used by urban neighbourhood groups.
The tradition is analysed as social capital that builds local cohesion but can also be exploited by local elites.
exampleEn: In a village near Cusco, families dig an irrigation channel in a single day of minka, eating a communal lunch of potatoes and corn while children carry water.
qualificationEn: Communal labour survives unevenly: Andean villages use it more than coastal cities, and politicians sometimes invoke minka for projects that are really paid work.

titleEn: Ciclovía and Bogotá's Sunday road revolution
facts: The ciclovía ("bike path") is a weekly event in Bogotá in which major roads are closed to motor traffic on Sunday mornings for cyclists, runners and walkers.
Bogotá's Ciclovía began in 1974 and now runs for about 120 kilometres on Sundays and public holidays, with millions of participants a year.
It is managed by the city's sports institute, with points where people can borrow bikes, get exercise advice and buy snacks.
The event reflects Bogotá's transport politics: it is championed as public space and health policy and defended by residents against proposals to shorten it.
Similar ciclovías spread across Latin America, in Mexico City, Guadalajara and Quito, and the model has been copied worldwide.
exampleEn: On a Sunday morning, a family in Bogotá cycles up Avenida Séptima with the mountains in view, stops at a fruit stand in a park and joins a free dance class on the closed asphalt.
qualificationEn: The ciclovía is managed by the city and varies by route; it is popular, but critics say the road closures disrupt access, and cycle infrastructure on other days is far less generous.

titleEn: Mateship and the Australian fair go
facts: Mateship is a central Australian cultural ideal: loyalty, equality and mutual support among friends, especially in hard conditions.
Its mythology comes from convicts, settlers, gold diggers, soldiers of the Anzac tradition and rural workers, for whom survival depended on mates.
The fair go is the related belief in equality of opportunity and a dislike of queue-jumpers and pretension, and tall poppy syndrome is its darker side.
Mateship is coded into national institutions through Anzac Day language, sporting teams, emergency volunteers and political rhetoric.
Critics note that the ideal historically excluded women, Indigenous Australians and migrants, and that it can slide into sexism and anti-intellectualism.
exampleEn: In a Queensland country town, a farmer's neighbours turn up with a ute and a toolbox after a flood, no invoice and no fuss, and a few weeks later the favour is returned.
qualificationEn: Mateship is a contested national story rather than a description of every friendship; urban life, multiculturalism and social media have changed how it is practised and invoked.

titleEn: Marae and the protocols of Māori community life
facts: Marae are the communal and ceremonial spaces of Māori community life: an open courtyard (marae ātea), a meeting house (wharenui), a dining hall and often a church.

The marae belongs to a hapū or whānau and is used for hui (meetings), tangihanga (funerals), weddings, birthdays and political debate, with protocols (tikanga) governing greetings, seating and speech-making.
The pōwhiri welcome moves visitors through the karanga call, speeches and the hongi, with visitors (manuhiri) and hosts (tangata whenua) separated on the courtyard.
Urban marae serve Māori living away from their ancestral lands, and marae-based health, education and training services are part of Māori community infrastructure.
Since the 2010s iwi settlements and government partnerships have funded marae repairs and earthquake strengthening.
exampleEn: At a Northland marae, a school group is welcomed with a karanga, then the visitors sit in rows while elders speak, and afterwards everyone shares a meal in the dining hall.
qualificationEn: Not all Māori are connected to a marae and not every meeting follows the full protocol; urban, rural and iwi differences matter, and the marae is a living institution rather than a heritage site.

titleEn: Kastom and the nakamal in Vanuatu
facts: Kastom is the Bislama word for customary law and tradition in Vanuatu, covering land tenure, marriage, ceremonies, dispute resolution and leadership.
Vanuatu's constitution recognises kastom as a source of law alongside introduced law, and the Malvatumauri National Council of Chiefs advises on customary matters.
Most land in Vanuatu is held under customary tenure, and disputes over land and family matters are often settled by chiefs rather than courts.
The nakamal is the traditional meeting house and communal space, especially in central Vanuatu, where kava is prepared and men gather for decisions and stories.
Urban life in Port Vila and Luganville has produced urban nakamals and kava bars, and chiefs' authority is contested by younger people, churches and the cash economy.
exampleEn: In a village on Efate, a land dispute comes before the chief in the nakamal; the men drink kava from a shared shell while the chief hears both families and announces a settlement.
qualificationEn: Kastom is not a single uniform code; it varies from island to island and has been reshaped by Christianity, colonial rule and the state, and urban ni-Vanuatu often live between customary and formal systems.
